fields.title: Data lifecycle
fields.keyTakeaway: Retention period is a product decision at the intersection of law, user value, and risk, and having no decision means choosing to "store forever".
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Data accumulates forever by default. Why is this bad and how to decide how much to store?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Eternal storage costs three times over: money for disks, query speed, risk in case of a leak. The third is more expensive than the first two combined because data leaks that no one has needed for a long time but are still sitting there. A product manager who did not ask about the retention period defaulted to "forever" — simply without noticing they were making a choice.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: Data cools down: the older it is, the less frequently it is accessed. Hence three temperatures.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Hot** — read constantly. Orders from the last month, active carts. Live in the main database on a fast disk.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Warm** — read occasionally. Orders from last year: the user occasionally checks history, accounting prepares a report. Can live in a separate partition or archive database, where it is slightly slower and noticeably cheaper.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **Cold** — almost never read, stored out of obligation. Accounting documents four years old. [[cold-storage|Cold storage]] is an order of magnitude cheaper than the main one, at the cost of minutes to retrieve.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: [[retention|Retention period]] is the rule determining how long data lives. Four forces define it, and the product manager must reconcile them:
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: *Law.* Financial documents are stored for a set period. Personal data, conversely, cannot be stored longer than necessary for the stated purpose.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: *Product.* How deep of a history does the user need? It often turns out that almost no one looks further than a year.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: *Analytics.* Year-over-year comparisons require data for at least two years.
fields.sections/2/blocks/8/text: *Cost and risk.* Every extra year is money and the volume of a potential leak.
fields.sections/2/blocks/9/text: The correct result is not a single period, but a table: each data type has its own term and its own fate upon expiration.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: An interesting consequence: anonymized orders older than three years continue to live in analytics because sums and categories are not personal data. This is how they met legal requirements without losing the ability to compare years. This is a compromise found by the product manager, not the lawyer and not the engineer: the lawyer demanded deletion, the engineer suggested deleting everything, and the product needed history.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Retention periods are easier to set than to actually comply with: data spreads across logs, exports, backups, and analyst tables. A policy without an inventory of storage locations is a document, not a practice.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Retention period is a product decision at the intersection of law, user value, and risk, and having no decision means choosing to "store forever".
